name: The Fast Fourier Transform
statement: Compute the frequencies in a signal in n log n time instead of n squared.
statementAccent: in n log n time instead of n squared
meaning: The fast Fourier transform, or FFT, is an algorithm that computes the discrete Fourier transform, or DFT, of a sequence, and its inverse, far more efficiently than the naive method. The discrete Fourier transform converts a finite sequence of samples, such as the values of a signal measured over time, into the amplitudes and phases of the frequencies that make it up, decomposing the signal into a sum of sinusoids. Computing the DFT directly from its definition takes on the order of n squared arithmetic operations for a sequence of n points, which becomes prohibitively slow for large n. The FFT reduces this to on the order of n log n operations by cleverly exploiting the structure and symmetries of the transform, recursively breaking a DFT into smaller DFTs. The most famous version, the Cooley-Tukey algorithm, was published by James Cooley and John Tukey in 1965 in the journal Mathematics of Computation, though the underlying idea was known earlier and traces back to Carl Friedrich Gauss around 1805. The dramatic speedup made frequency analysis practical on real signals and turned the Fourier transform into a routine computational tool. The mathematician Gilbert Strang called the FFT the most important numerical algorithm of our lifetime, and in 2000 it was named one of the top ten algorithms of the twentieth century. The FFT is fundamental to digital signal processing and appears throughout technology, in audio and image compression such as MP3 and JPEG, in telecommunications, and in scientific computing.
mechanism: The FFT achieves its speed by recursively decomposing a discrete Fourier transform into smaller transforms and reusing intermediate results, replacing redundant computation with a divide-and-conquer structure. The DFT of n points is a sum that, computed directly, requires about n multiplications for each of n outputs, giving order n squared work. The Cooley-Tukey algorithm, in its most common radix-2 form, assumes n is a power of two and splits the sequence into its even-indexed and odd-indexed samples, computes the DFT of each half, and then combines them using the periodicity and symmetry of the complex exponential factors, the so-called twiddle factors. Because each of those half-size DFTs can be split again in the same way, the recursion continues down to trivial one-point transforms, producing about log n levels, each requiring order n work to combine, for a total of order n log n operations. This exponential-to-polynomial-in-log improvement is what makes the difference: for a million points, the naive DFT needs on the order of a trillion operations while the FFT needs only tens of millions. Many variants exist beyond the radix-2 case, handling composite and prime sizes, real-valued input, and multiple dimensions, but all share the strategy of factoring the transform into smaller pieces. The idea was rediscovered several times, and its history reaches back to Gauss, but Cooley and Tukey's 1965 paper, appearing as digital computers made large transforms feasible, brought it into universal use and set off the field of digital signal processing.

examples.text: Radix-2 Cooley-Tukey splits a DFT into even and odd samples, transforms each, and combines with twiddle factors.
For a million points the naive DFT needs about a trillion operations; the FFT needs only tens of millions.
The FFT underlies audio and image compression such as MP3 and JPEG and modern telecommunications.

whyItMatters: The fast Fourier transform is one of the most consequential algorithms ever devised, the tool that made frequency analysis a practical, everyday operation rather than a computational luxury. By reducing the cost of the discrete Fourier transform from order n squared to order n log n, it turned problems that would have taken impossibly long into ones solvable in an instant, and in doing so it created the field of digital signal processing and reshaped science and engineering. Its reach is extraordinary: the FFT is what lets computers compress audio into MP3s and images into JPEGs, transmit data over wireless and broadband networks using techniques like OFDM, filter and analyze sounds and images, process medical scans, and carry out large-scale numerical simulations and multiplications. The mathematician Gilbert Strang called it the most important numerical algorithm of our lifetime, and in 2000 an expert panel named it among the ten algorithms with the greatest influence on the development of science and engineering in the twentieth century. That its essential idea reaches back to Gauss, yet found universal use only when Cooley and Tukey published it in 1965 as computers came of age, is a striking illustration of how algorithm and hardware together transform what is possible. As the method that computes frequencies in n log n time, the FFT is foundational to the digital world.

working.text: start from the discrete Fourier transform, which decomposes a signal into its frequencies.
divide the sequence into even and odd parts and transform each, down to one-point transforms.
merge the sub-transforms using twiddle factors, giving order n log n total work.

limits: The FFT is a computational method, not a different transform, and several points reward care. It computes the same discrete Fourier transform as the naive method, only faster, so any limitation of the DFT itself, such as spectral leakage from finite windows or the assumption of periodicity, still applies. The classic radix-2 Cooley-Tukey algorithm is simplest when n is a power of two, and while variants handle arbitrary sizes, performance can vary with the factorization of n, prime lengths being least convenient. The order n log n figure is an operation count that ignores constant factors, memory access patterns, and numerical precision, all of which matter in practice, and good FFT libraries optimize heavily for particular hardware. The history rewards care: the essential idea was described by Gauss around 1805 and rediscovered several times, so crediting the FFT solely to Cooley and Tukey in 1965 overlooks Gauss and others, even though the 1965 paper was what brought it into general use. The Strang quotation and the top-ten-algorithms recognition should be attributed accurately. So the FFT robustly computes the DFT in order n log n time, understood as an efficient algorithm for an existing transform with a long and layered history.
misreadings: The FFT is not a new kind of transform but a fast way to compute the discrete Fourier transform, so it inherits the DFT's assumptions and artifacts. It was not invented from nothing in 1965; Gauss knew the idea around 1805, and Cooley and Tukey brought it into wide use. And order n log n counts operations, not real-world time, which depends on constants and hardware, so treating the FFT as a distinct transform, as wholly original to 1965, or as free of all cost, misreads it.
origin: The algorithm for computing the discrete Fourier transform in order n log n time, published by Cooley and Tukey in 1965 with roots in Gauss around 1805, foundational to digital signal processing.
